thread.title: Qualcomm: Apple, Samsung Custom Chips a Growing Risk, Says Wells

author: Barron's
title: Qualcomm: Apple, Samsung Custom Chips a Growing Risk, Says Wells
text:
Apple Inc. The rise of custom chips by Apple ( AAPL ) and other electronics giants is a risk to chip makers such as Qualcomm ( QCOM ), writes Wells Fargo analyst David Wong in a note to clients yesterday afternoon.
Wong is referring to parts such as the " A11 Bionic " processor running Apple 's ( AAPL ) iPhone X , which is designed by Apple and used only by itself, a practice known in the industry as a " captive " part, versus chips sold on the open market for use by anyone, known as " merchant " sales.
In addition to an overall slowing smartphone market Wong writes that, "we think that the growing using of internally designed chips by the biggest smartphone companies is creating a headwind to growth for merchant chip companies that make smartphone applications processors and baseband chips," writes Wong.
Wong maintains a Neutral rating on Qualcomm stock.
Relying on data from research firm Strategy Analytics , he estimates that a third of the entire "applications processor" sales into smartphones is taken up by captive chips, including Apple's A-series processors but also Samsung Electronics 's ( 005930KS ) home-grown " Exynos " processors, which power an increasing percentage of the South Korean giant's phones; and privately held Huawei 's " Kirin " chip for its devices. Samsung sells Exynos to other manufacturers to a limited extent, writes Wong.
The market for merchant chips such as Qualcomm's has consolidated to a three-horse race between that company and Taiwan's MediaTek ( 2454TW ) and China's Spreadtrum .
The risk is that Apple and Samsung and Huawei may not only expand use of the chips, but also expand their capabilities . They might, for example, displace not just Qualcomm's apps processors but also the other major chip in a smartphone, the baseband modem processor:
We think it remains an open question as to whether Apple will continue to use standalone modems from Qualcomm and/or Intel, or whether Apple will attempt to integrate modem capability onto its processor chip in the future.
Samsung's early Exynos chips did not have integrated modems. We think that in 2013 and 2014 Samsung stepped up its use of integrated modem/processor chips such as Qualcomm's Snapdragon chip, purchased from merchant chipmakers. We believe that with the availability of Exynos processors that had integrated modems Samsung has increased its use of its own Eyxnos chips in its smartphones in recent years […] the fact that Samsung now has its own integrate processor/modem versions of Exynos gives it more flexibility to increase the proportion of smartphones using Exynos in the future, if it decides to do so. We think that Huawei's consumption of about 20 million Kirin chips per quarter 2 | Wells Fargo Securities, LLC Wireless Handset Chips Equity Research demonstrates Huawei's satisfaction with its own chip and likely justifies enough continuing investment in chip development to give Kirin and its successors a good chance of remaining competitive with merchant solutions.
Wong contemplates the possibility both that Apple will use Intel ( INTC ) not only as a second source to Qualcomm for baseband chips, as it does now, but also for future foundry services to make a custom integrated application processor and baseband modem:
Intel has both foundry capability and an organization that can offer design support to integrate Intel's modem circuitry into a foundry customer's chips. On February 22, 2018 Intel announced an alliance with Unigroup Spreadtrum & RDA in which the two companies would develop a 5G solution utilizing an Intel modem (XMM 8000 series) and Spreadtrum's application processor capabilities. The collaboration targets offering 5G modem chips to the Chinese handset market by the 2H19 timeframe. Admittedly Intel has a minority ownership stake in the Tsinghua Unigroup holding company that owns Spreadtrum so Spreadtrum may well have a predisposition to work with Intel where possible. If at some point in the future Apple decided to tap into Intel's foundry and modem capabilities to design a chip that integrated Apples A-series processor with Intel's modem circuitry, manufactured at Intel as a foundry, this could impact Qualcomm's modem sales into iPhone, while potential benefiting Intel even though Intel could also lose its own standalone modem sales into iPhone. Alternatively, if Apple decided not to attempt to develop its own integrated processor/modem chip, we think there is always the possibility that Apple might go back to using modems from Qualcomm exclusively in some future iPhone generation.
Qualcomm is set to report earnings Wednesday April 25 , after the closing bell.
Qualcomm shares are down 2 cents at $50.51.
